title: You Asked God to Heal the Wound. He Never Asked You to Pretend It Didn’t Hurt.
paragraphs: You Asked God to Heal the Wound. He Never Asked You to Pretend It Didn’t Hurt.
Maybe faith was never supposed to make you pretend the wound wasn’t real. Maybe the God you have been trying to look strong for has been standing closer to your broken heart than you realized.
There is a particular kind of pain Christians sometimes become very good at hiding.
You know how to worship while carrying it.
You know when to say, “God is good.”
You know which verse to quote.
You know how to smile when someone asks how you are doing.
You know how to lift your hands in church while part of your heart is quietly asking a question you are almost ashamed to admit:
“Jesus… why does this still hurt?”
You prayed.
You forgave—or you are trying to.
You opened your Bible.
You asked God to heal you.
Months passed.
Maybe years.
And somehow the wound still knows your name.
A song can find it.
A photograph can find it.
An empty chair can find it.
A familiar street can find it.
A date on the calendar can find it.
Sometimes one innocent sentence from another person touches the place you thought had finally stopped bleeding, and suddenly you are fighting tears nobody else understands.
Then comes another pain on top of the original pain.
Guilt.
Shouldn't I be over this by now?
If I really trusted God, wouldn't I be stronger?
If I truly forgave, why can I still remember?
Why am I grieving when everyone else seems to have moved on?
And perhaps somewhere along the way, you began confusing healing with pretending.
But Scripture never asks you to call a wound painless when it hurts.
Psalm 34:18 says:
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted and saves the crushed in spirit.”
The Hebrew is breathtaking:
קָרוֹב יְהוָה לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי־לֵב
Qārōv YHWH lenishberê-lēv.
“The LORD is near to the brokenhearted.”
That word translated “brokenhearted” comes from the Hebrew root שָׁבַר — shāvar, carrying the idea of breaking, shattering, or crushing.
Notice what David does not say.
He does not say the brokenhearted are embarrassing to God.
He does not say God stands at a distance until they become emotionally presentable.
He does not say, “Stop crying and prove your faith.”
He says:
קָרוֹב — qārōv.
Near.
That changes everything.
God does not merely tolerate the brokenhearted.
He draws near.
And the context matters.

Psalm 34 is traditionally connected with one of David's humiliating escapes from danger. The superscription recalls David altering his behavior before Abimelech, being driven away, and escaping—an episode corresponding to the account involving Achish in 1 Samuel 21.
This is not poetry floating above real life.
It was praise written in the shadow of fear, danger, humiliation, and deliverance.
David knew what it meant to be afraid.
In Psalm 34:4 he says that he sought the LORD and was delivered from his fears.
Later he speaks of the righteous having many afflictions.
Many.
Biblical faith does not require us to erase that word.
Scripture does not teach that belonging to God means never being wounded. It teaches us where the wounded can go.
And sometimes that is precisely where religious pretending becomes dangerous.
Because you can become so committed to appearing healed that you stop bringing the actual wound to the Healer.
You tell everyone, “I'm fine.”
But you're not.
You say, “It doesn't bother me anymore.”
But it does.
You insist, “I've moved on.”
Then you lie awake at 2:13 in the morning replaying the conversation.
You post the verse.
You encourage everybody else.
You answer prayer requests.
You serve.
You worship.
You laugh.
And then you go somewhere nobody can see you…
and fall apart.
Listen carefully.
Falling apart in the presence of God is not the same thing as abandoning faith.
Sometimes lament is faith refusing to run anywhere else.
The Bible contains an entire vocabulary for suffering because God apparently never intended His people to become strangers to honest grief.
“Why, O LORD, do you stand far away?” cries Psalm 10:1.
“How long, O LORD?” asks Psalm 13:1.
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” begins Psalm 22:1.
These words are not preserved in Scripture so we can shame hurting people for feeling them.
They are Scripture.
God gave His people language for the nights when ordinary language fails.
And then something staggering happens in the Gospel.
Jesus Himself takes the opening cry of Psalm 22 upon His lips at the cross.
Ἠλί Ἠλί λεμὰ σαβαχθανί
Ēli Ēli lema sabachthani?
Matthew 27:46 records the anguished cry and explains it:
“My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?”
Jesus was not sinning by expressing anguish.
He was suffering.
The sinless Son of God did not turn agony into a performance of emotional cheerfulness.
And before Calvary, standing at the tomb of Lazarus, Scripture gives us one of its shortest and most devastating sentences:
ἐδάκρυσεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς.
Edakrysen ho Iēsous.

“Jesus wept.”
John 11:35.
Think about that.
Jesus knew resurrection was coming.
He knew Lazarus would walk out of that tomb.
And Jesus still wept.
Hope did not make tears unnecessary.
Knowledge of what God would do next did not make present grief unreal.
That means your tears are not automatically evidence that your faith has failed.
Grief and hope can occupy the same heart.
A Christian can know that Christ is risen and still miss someone who died.
A believer can forgive and still need time for damaged trust to be rebuilt wisely.
A person can believe God is good while grieving something terrible that happened.
A wounded Christian can seek prayer, pastoral care, mature friendship, and when appropriate professional support without betraying dependence upon God.
Scripture itself repeatedly pictures God's people carrying burdens together.
“Bear one another's burdens,” Paul tells believers in Galatians 6:2.
James tells suffering believers to pray.
Romans tells Christians to “weep with those who weep.”
Not lecture them into smiling.
Not rush them through grief.
Not turn their suffering into a theological examination they must pass before receiving compassion.
Weep.
With.
Them.
Maybe someone needed to do that for you.
Maybe instead they told you to get over it.
Maybe somebody spiritualized the wound because sitting beside your pain made them uncomfortable.
Maybe they handed you Romans 8:28 before they gave you permission to cry.
Romans 8:28 is gloriously true.
But truth is not meant to be used as a weapon against grief.
The same Paul who wrote about God working all things together for good also described creation as groaning.
He described believers as groaning.
He spoke of weakness.
He spoke of suffering.
And Romans 8 does not end by pretending suffering is imaginary.
It ends by proclaiming that suffering cannot separate God's people from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
That is a far stronger hope.
Christianity does not say:
“Nothing hurts.”
Christianity says:
Nothing—not even what hurts—can separate those who are in Christ from His love.
There is a difference.
And perhaps that is why you have been exhausted.
You haven't only been carrying the wound.
You have been carrying the performance.
Trying to convince everybody that what happened didn't change you.
Trying to prove that you forgave.
Trying to look victorious.
Trying not to make anybody uncomfortable.
Trying to be the “strong Christian.”
But Jesus never asked you to become your own savior.
He already took that position.
There is a strange freedom in finally praying:
“Lord, this hurt me.”
Not accusing God.
Not worshiping the wound.
Not making pain your identity.
Just telling the truth in His presence.
“Jesus, I still miss them.”
“Jesus, I am angry.”
“Jesus, I don't understand.”
“Jesus, I forgave them, but I am still rebuilding.”
“Jesus, I thought I would be farther along by now.”
“Jesus, I'm tired.”
“Jesus, help me.”
That last prayer may be more faithful than a thousand counterfeit smiles.
Because grace begins where pretending ends.
And this is where the Gospel becomes more than inspirational language.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to improve your mood.
He came to save sinners.
Our deepest problem is greater than emotional pain: sin has alienated humanity from our holy God, and no amount of self-improvement can reconcile us to Him.
Yet God did what we could never do for ourselves.
Christ entered our broken world.
He lived without sin.
He bore sin at the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose again.
The Christian message is not that sufficiently wounded people can rescue themselves.
It is that a crucified and risen Savior rescues sinners who cannot rescue themselves.
So bring Him more than your wound.
Bring Him your sin.
Bring the bitterness you have secretly fed.
Bring the hatred.
Bring the unbelief.
Bring the compromises you justified because somebody hurt you first.
Bring the secret habits you used to numb what you didn't want to feel.
Bring the pride that keeps saying, “I can handle this myself.”
Bring everything into the light.
Repentance is not God humiliating wounded people.
It is His call to turn from sin and come home to Him.
And forgiveness is not God announcing that sin never mattered.
Look at the cross.
Sin mattered enough that redemption cost the blood of Christ.
Grace is not denial.
Grace tells the truth about our sin and then points us to the Savior whose mercy is greater.
That is why the cross can hold truths we often tear apart.
You were genuinely hurt.
And you may also genuinely need repentance.
Someone may have sinned against you.
And your response to that sin may have grown sinful too.
What happened to you may not have been your choice.
What you do with your heart before God still matters.
Jesus can confront the sinner and comfort the wounded person without confusing either one.
Sometimes He is doing both in the same human heart.
Maybe yours.
This is where scandal becomes grace.
Not because Jesus rewrites history as though evil never happened.
He does something far greater.
He redeems people evil tried to destroy.
Joseph could eventually say of those who betrayed him, “You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.”
Joseph did not call evil good.
He called it evil.
Then he confessed that evil did not have the final word.
That is biblical redemption.
Your scars may remain part of your story without remaining the author of your story.
The betrayal does not get the last sentence.
The divorce does not get the last sentence.
The abandonment does not get the last sentence.
The funeral does not get the last sentence.
The abuse does not get the last sentence.
The failure does not get the last sentence.
The years you lost do not get the last sentence.
Your own worst sin does not have to get the last sentence if you come to Christ in repentance and faith.
Jesus does.
And resurrection means God specializes in endings human beings could never have written.
But please hear this carefully:
Healing is not always instant.
The Bible does not give us permission to promise that every emotional wound disappears on our preferred timetable.
Sometimes God delivers dramatically.
Sometimes restoration unfolds slowly through prayer, Scripture, wise community, boundaries, forgiveness, counsel, repeated surrender, and years of learning to walk in truth.
Sometimes consequences remain even where forgiveness is real.
Sometimes reconciliation is possible.
Sometimes wisdom requires distance.
Forgiveness and unrestricted access are not identical.
Trust can require rebuilding.
And lament may visit again without meaning you have returned to the beginning.
A scar aching does not mean the wound is still controlling you.
Sometimes it simply reminds you that something happened there.
So when the memory returns, you don't have to panic.
You can say:
“Yes, Lord. That still hurts.
And You are still here.”
קָרוֹב יְהוָה.
Qārōv YHWH.
The LORD is near.
Near when you cannot explain yourself.
Near when worship comes through tears.
Near when you need somebody trustworthy to sit beside you.
Near when yesterday unexpectedly enters today.
Near when healing feels painfully slow.
Near when you finally stop saying, “I'm okay,” and whisper what heaven already knows:
“I'm hurting.”
Perhaps this article found you because you have spent too long apologizing for being human.
So don't perform for God tonight.
Pray.
Tell Him what hurts.
Confess what is sinful.
Ask for wisdom about what needs boundaries.
Ask for courage where forgiveness is required.
Ask for trustworthy believers who will carry the burden with you.
Seek appropriate pastoral or professional help when the weight is more than you know how to carry alone.
Open the Psalms and discover that Scripture is not frightened by tears.
Then look toward Jesus.
Not merely as an example of suffering.
As Savior.
The Man of Sorrows who went through death and emerged victorious.
The Lamb who was slain.
The risen King.

The One who does not merely make wounded people feel temporarily better but reconciles sinners to God and promises His people a future in which death, mourning, crying, and pain will finally be no more.
That day is coming.
Until then, Christianity gives us something stronger than pretending.
Presence.
Hope.
Truth.
Grace.
Christ.
They post normally.
They laugh.
They go to work.
They attend church.
Nobody knows that after everyone goes to sleep, the wound starts talking again.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor. It doesn't.
It cannot.
Christ cannot be bought.
But glorifying God includes making His truth known, serving others, supporting faithful Gospel work according to our ability, and refusing to hide the hope we have received.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks continuing pain means God is disappointed in them.
Tell the truth.
Someone reading beneath this article may need evidence that wounded people can keep walking with Jesus.
Let the comments become more than engagement.
Let them become a place where believers bear one another's burdens.
Where somebody discovers they aren't the only one still grieving.
Where somebody who has been hiding finally asks for prayer.
Where somebody who wandered remembers that Jesus is still calling sinners home.
Because perhaps the most painful mistake you made was believing God would only come near after you stopped looking broken.
Psalm 34 says the opposite.
He is near to the brokenhearted.
So stop handing Jesus the edited version of your heart.
Give Him the bleeding one.
Give Him the frightened one.
Give Him the angry one.
Give Him the ashamed one.
Give Him the exhausted one.
Give Him the sinful one in repentance.
Give Him the heart that still doesn't understand why it happened.
And let the Savior meet you in truth.
You asked God to heal the wound.
He never asked you to pretend it didn't hurt.
The wound may explain some of your tears—but because of Jesus, it does not get to write the ending.
